title: Sounding natural
goal: React like a local, add "right?" and "isn't it?" to what you say, stress words with ته, ئي and به, use the paired words Sindhis love, ask what a word means or ask people to slow down, and mix in English the way everyone does.
intro:
You can now say almost anything in correct Sindhi. This unit is about saying it the way people **actually** talk: the little words that carry attitude. A Sindhi friend doesn't just say 'you're coming tomorrow' — they say **تون سڀاڻي ايندين نه؟** 'you're coming tomorrow, **right**?'. They don't just say 'look' — they say **ڏس ته سهي!** 'just **look**!'. They react with **توبه!**, **شاباس!**, **ڇا ٿو چوين!**, and they talk about **ڳالهه ٻولهه** and **ڀڄ ڊڪ** — pairs of words that mean 'chatting and all that', 'rushing about and all that'.

You'll also learn the fast-speech **آ** for آهي, how to ask what a word means or to slow down — and the fact that mixing English (and Urdu) into Sindhi is completely normal.

grammar.title: Tag questions: … نه؟, ها نه؟, ٺيڪ؟
grammar.body:
English has a whole system of tags (*isn't it, aren't you, didn't they*). Sindhi just adds one little word at the end, with a rising voice:

**نه؟** (na) — the all-purpose tag: تون ايندين **نه؟** 'you're coming, aren't you?', توهان سنڌي سمجهو ٿا **نه؟** 'you understand Sindhi, don't you?'
**آهي نه؟** / **آ نه؟** — 'isn't it?' after a comment: گرمي ڏاڍي آ، **آهي نه؟** 'it's really hot, isn't it?'
**ها نه؟** — 'yeah? right?', looking for agreement: مزو آيو، **ها نه؟**
**ٺيڪ؟** / **صحيح؟** — 'OK? right?', checking a plan: ستين وڳي، **ٺيڪ؟**
**سمجهيو؟** / **سمجهين ٿو؟** — 'got it? you see?'

The tag never changes for person, tense or negative — the same نه works everywhere. After a **negative** statement, people usually add **ته** to the statement and keep the voice rising: تون ناراض **ته** ناهين؟ 'you're not upset, are you?'

**Answering**: ها / هائو 'yes (you're right)' agrees with the statement; نه نه 'no, no' disagrees. To an elder: جي ها / جي سائين.

**Don't confuse** this tag نه with the نه that softens a command (اچ نه! 'do come!', unit 21) — the tag comes after a statement and rises; the softener comes after a command and falls.

grammar.title: Emphasis: ته, ئي, به, ته سهي — and ڪيڏو نه!
grammar.body:
Sindhi adds emphasis with small particles placed **right after** the word you want to stress:

**ته** (ta) — 'as for…, at least, really'. It sets a word against others or adds attitude: **مان ته** ويندس 'well, **I'm** going (whatever you do)'; هي **ته** ڌوڪو آهي! 'this is a scam, plain and simple!'; ٺيڪ **ته** آهي 'it's fine, really'.

**ئي** (ī) — 'exactly, just, only, right': هتي **ئي** 'right here', اهو **ئي** 'that very one', هاڻي **ئي** 'right now', مان **ئي** 'only me / me myself'. اهو ئي ته مسئلو آهي 'that's exactly the problem'.

**به** (bi) — 'also', but in negative sentences 'not even': هن کي پنهنجو نمبر **به** ياد ناهي 'he doesn't **even** remember his own number'; ڪڏهن **به** نه 'never ever'.

**ته سهي** — after an informal command, it means 'just (do it)', urging and friendly at once: ڏس **ته سهي** 'just look', ٻڌ **ته سهي** 'just listen'. Similarly verb + ته + ڏس means 'try it': کائي ته ڏس 'just try (eating) it'.

**Exclamations** with **ڪيڏو / ڪيڏي / ڪيڏا** 'how (much)!', usually with **نه**: **ڪيڏو نه** سهڻو شهر آهي! 'what a beautiful city!'; **ڪيڏي نه** گرمي آهي! 'it's so hot!'. ڪيڏو agrees with the noun.

The trap: these particles only work **after** their word. ته مان ويندس means 'then I'll go' (ته = then), not 'I for one will go'.

grammar.title: Paired words and echo words: ڳالهه ٻولهه, ٺيڪ ٺاڪ
grammar.body:
Spoken Sindhi loves **pairs**. Two words with similar meanings are joined to mean 'X and all that goes with it'. They sound warm and natural, and you'll hear them in every conversation:

ڳالهه ٻولهه — talk + speech = conversation, chatting
پڇا ڳاڇا — asking + asking = enquiries
ڀڄ ڊڪ — running + running = rushing about
گهر ٻار — house + children = home and family
مٽ مائٽ — relatives + relatives = the whole extended family
اوڙو پاڙو — the neighbourhood, all the neighbours
ڪم ڪار — work and chores (unit 26)
چانهه پاڻي — tea + water = refreshments, 'tea or something'
ٿورو گهڻو — little + much = a bit, more or less

A few are **echo words**, where the second half just repeats the first with a changed vowel: **ٺيڪ ٺاڪ** 'OK, alright-ish'. The echo makes the word vaguer and more casual: ٺيڪ 'fine' → ٺيڪ ٺاڪ 'fine, sort of'.

**How they behave**: the pair acts as **one word** — one gender, one set of endings. Both halves take the oblique together: مٽ مائٽ → **مٽن مائٽن** کي; اوڙو پاڙو → **اوڙي پاڙي** ۾. Don't put ۽ 'and' between them: ڳالهه ۽ ٻولهه sounds wrong.

Use them in relaxed speech; in formal writing, the single word (ڳالهه، رشتيدار…) is more usual.

culture:
**Mixing is normal.** Educated Sindhis, especially in Karachi and Hyderabad, slide between Sindhi, Urdu and English in a single sentence: *ميٽنگ ڪينسل ٿي وئي، so مان free آهيان*. English nouns and verbs + ڪرڻ / ٿيڻ are simply part of the language (unit 34), and nobody will think your Sindhi is worse for using them. Purists and older people in villages use more Sindhi and Persian-Arabic words — respect it, but don't feel you must speak 'pure' Sindhi.

**Accents**: the standard is the central **Vicholi** of Hyderabad and the media; **Lari** in the south (Thatta, Badin) and **Siroli** in the north (Sukkur, Larkana, Jacobabad) sound noticeably different, as does the Sindhi of Thar and of Kutch in India. People enjoy guessing where you learned yours.

**When you're learning**, Sindhis are delighted to hear their language from a foreigner — and will often switch to Urdu or English to 'help'. Say kindly: **مهرباني ڪري سنڌي ۾ ڳالهايو، مان سکي رهيو آهيان**. Ask about words freely; people love explaining, and a question like **هن لفظ جو مطلب ڇا آهي؟** often starts a long and warm conversation.

**Tone**: reactions are lively — **توبه!**, **ڇا ٿو چوين!**, **شاباس!** — but keep اڙي and تون-forms for friends. With elders, add **سائين** and use توهان, even when the reaction is the same.

tip.title: Reactions, by register
tip.body:
- With friends: **اڙي!** 'hey!', **ڇا ٿو چوين!** 'no way!', **شاباس!** 'well done!'
- Shock: **توبه!**; annoyance: **اوهو!**; impossible: **ناممڪن!**
- Great: **زبردست!**; rubbish: **بيڪار**.
- With elders: ڇا ٿا چئو! and add سائين.

tip.title: Tags: … نه؟
tip.body:
- Add **نه؟** with a rising voice: تون ايندين **نه؟** 'you're coming, right?'
- **آ نه؟ / آهي نه؟** 'isn't it?', **ها نه؟** 'yeah?', **ٺيڪ؟** 'OK?'
- The tag never changes.
- Fast speech: **آ** = آهي: ڇا حال **آ**؟

tip.title: ته, ئي, به, ته سهي
tip.body:
- **ته** after a word = 'as for, really': **مان ته** ويندس.
- **ئي** = exactly, just: هتي **ئي**، اهو **ئي**.
- **به** in a negative = not even: نمبر **به** ياد ناهي.
- **ته سهي** after a command = just…: ڏس **ته سهي**!
- **ڪيڏو نه** …! = how …!
tip.pattern: word + ته / ئي / به · command + ته سهي

tip.title: Paired words
tip.body:
- Two words, one meaning 'X and all that': **ڳالهه ٻولهه** chatting, **ڀڄ ڊڪ** rushing about, **پڇا ڳاڇا** enquiries.
- Echo word: **ٺيڪ ٺاڪ** 'OK-ish'.
- The pair is one word: one gender, no ۽ in the middle.

sentences.roman: oṛe pāṛe vārā sabhu shādīa te āyā.
sentences.en: All the neighbours came to the wedding.
I understand a bit, more or less. (man)
At least eat a little something!

sentences.native: هن جو گهر ٻار ڪراچيءَ ۾ آهي.
sentences.roman: hun jo ghara ɓāru karāchīa meṃ āhe.
sentences.en: His family lives in Karachi.
Did you tell the relatives?

sentences.native: اوڙي پاڙي ۾ سڀني کي خبر آهي.
sentences.roman: oṛe pāṛe meṃ sabhinī khe xabara āhe.
sentences.en: Everyone in the neighbourhood knows.
